extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, naturalists, scientific reviewers and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative commentary for reviewing scientific or popular-science books and practical reports, emphasizing fairness, accuracy, evidence-checking, attribution, and usefulness to practitioners. Also includes criteria for judging practical manuals and official scientific reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and evidence-checking by the critic
rubrics_metrics.description: The question for the critic, in judging the work of the self-appointed public instructor, is whether he deals fairly with his public, carefully weighing and testing for them the data which they cannot weigh and test for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reviewer should act as a surrogate for the general reader by critically evaluating the evidence and arguments the author presents, not merely repeating claims. Check that broad assertions are supported by evidence accessible or understandable to readers; point out where the author fails to weigh or test data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in factual and technical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must correctly use technical terms and distinctions (example: distinction between dolmens and single upright standing stones/menhirs); failure to do so is a sign of weak scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify specialized terminology and typologies (archaeology, taxonomy, etc.). Cite counter-examples from primary literature if author misidentifies or conflates types. Anti-pattern: treating distinct categories as identical (e.g., calling cromlechs/menhirs ‘stone tables’ without recognizing differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reliable sources and avoidance of worthless or unverified reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not support views by relying on 'worthless remarks' or single unreliable statements (example: accepting an anecdotal statement about a language community as authoritative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check ethnographic, historical, or other anecdotal claims against established authorities and multiple sources (e.g., prefer Burton over a single unverified traveler’s remark). Flag when an author's evidence is based on hearsay or discredited observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-checking historical and geographical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical statements should be checked against contemporary accounts and primary sources; avoid repeating untrustworthy secondary accounts or conflating distinct places (example: confusing Marian and Ladrone Islands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm dates, place-names, and primary-source testimony rather than relying on later retellings. When an asserted fact contradicts primary records, point it out and provide corrective references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attribution and acknowledgment of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should make particular acknowledgment to the writers whose facts and ideas they incorporate; omission can mislead readers about originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author credits sources for facts, quotations, and ideas. A reviewer should note failures to acknowledge prior work, as this affects the author's intellectual honesty and readers' understanding of provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and suitability of exposition for the target audience
rubrics_metrics.description: For popular exposition, the author should make the text readable for the general public without sacrificing essential accuracy (example: collecting detailed materials into an Appendix to keep the main text readable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prose is accessible to the intended readership and whether technical details are placed appropriately (e.g., main text vs appendix). Anti-pattern: oversimplifying to the point of inaccuracy, or packing essential evidence only in inaccessible appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and comprehensiveness of practical instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical manuals should direct practitioners through all necessary operations (example: a fruit-tree manual 'professes to direct the gardener in all the operations necessary, from the insertion of the graft to the completion of the tree').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the work covers the full sequence of practical steps and techniques relevant to its topic (grafting, pruning, training modes, etc.). Note omissions or superficial treatment of important procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to local conditions and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical guidance should be adapted or modified for the intended cultivators or readers (example: portions adapted for French cultivators modified for English readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether authors tailor recommendations, varieties, or cultural practices to local climates, soils, and customs. Effective manuals explain where local modification is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations and visual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative material (woodcuts, lithograms) is valuable in explanatory and practical works; well-executed plates and figures enhance usability and comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess quality, relevance, and sufficiency of figures and plates. For practical or taxonomic works, images that clarify morphology or steps in a procedure are important; low-quality or missing illustrations are deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical applicability and relevance to practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific or entomological reports should have a definite practical bearing on the welfare of the community (example: state reports giving causes of pests and best antidotes, leading to material improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether research or reports translate into actionable recommendations for growers, farmers, or policy (cause identification, remedies, cultivation advice). Favor work that connects scientific findings to practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness, scope, and organization of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Good official reports are thorough, well-organized, and cover relevant categories (example: sections on insects injurious to apple, grape, wheat, potato, cabbage, etc., with illustrations and experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the report systematically addresses the major topics, includes experimental results, distributional data, and is organized to be usable by stakeholders. Check for breadth (multiple crops/pests) and depth (experimental details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness and caution in practical recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions and practical advice should reflect realistic economic and practical considerations (example: advising against large-scale silk-culture yet recognizing small-scale viability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether recommendations acknowledge economic realities, limitations, and context; flag over-optimistic or unqualified endorsements. Prefer balanced conclusions that advise caution where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public funding and orientation toward public benefit (policy criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research with large public benefits but limited direct profitability may warrant public support to turn scientific work to practical account (argument for state encouragement of botanists and entomologists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutional reports or programs, consider whether public funding and organization are appropriate to enable research that yields community-level returns though not lucrative for individual investigators.
